html:
The spread of cocoa farming across the forests of southern Ivory Coast after independence, which by the late 1970s made the country the largest cocoa producer in the world. It still is, with about 40 percent of world supply.

Houphouet-Boigny said the land belongs to whoever farms it, and migrants from Upper Volta and Mali cleared forest for new farms. Fast growth in the 1960s and 1970s was called the Ivorian miracle. When world prices fell in the late 1980s, the state ran into debt and austerity, and fights over land and the rights of migrants grew. Most of the forest is gone, and child labour on farms is a lasting concern of the world chocolate trade. See also cocoa in Ghana.
